question: Inhibin: a new circulating marker of hydatidiform mole?
answer: Serum inhibin was significantly higher in patients with complete hydatidiform mole before evacuation than in normal pregnant women at the same stage (median 8.3 vs 2.8 U/ml). It fell significantly 7-10 days after evacuation to levels like those in the normal follicular phase, and molar tissue contained high inhibin concentrations. None of the four patients whose post-evacuation serum inhibin was 0.4 U/ml or less developed persistent trophoblastic disease, which suggests possible prognostic value. In patients with hydatidiform mole, invasive mole or choriocarcinoma, inhibin A was raised in 10/17 patients and inhibin B in 4/17, while HCG and HCGbeta were high in all. Inhibin A tracked HCG and HCGbeta during chemotherapy and normalized faster than HCG in some patients, whereas inhibin B did not correlate with HCGbeta.

question: Discharging patients earlier from Winnipeg hospitals: does it adversely affect quality of care?
answer: In Winnipeg's seven large acute care hospitals, length of stay fell significantly over 1989-90 to 1992-93 (11.1% for AMI to 22.0% for bronchitis/asthma) without a consistent rise in 30-day readmissions for AMI, bronchitis/asthma, or TURP, so earlier discharge did not appear to adversely affect quality of care. Readmission for uterine or adnexal procedures rose significantly between the first and second year (p=0.04) but then stayed constant over the next three years. Mean physician visits after discharge changed little (a slight rise for AMI in year one, a slight fall for bronchitis/asthma). Across individual Winnipeg hospitals in 1992-93, length of stay was not significantly correlated with readmission rates in any of the four categories, nor with physician visits for AMI and bronchitis/asthma.

question: Transesophageal echocardiographic assessment of left ventricular function in brain-dead patients: are marginally acceptable hearts suitable for transplantation?
answer: In a prospective study of 55 potential brain-dead heart donors assessed by transesophageal echocardiography, 36 of 40 harvested hearts were successfully transplanted, including 9 from donors with a fractional area change (FAC) below 50%, suggesting marginal left ventricular function does not preclude successful transplantation. Actuarial survival at 1 and 2 years was 86.2% versus 64.6% for recipients of hearts from donors with FAC over 50% versus below 50%, a difference that was not statistically significant. In 18 hearts assessed by TEE in both donor and recipient, FAC rose significantly from 51% to 57%, indicating that donor dysfunction can improve after transplantation.

question: Vertical lines in distal esophageal mucosa (VLEM): a true endoscopic manifestation of esophagitis in children?
answer: In a retrospective review of pediatric esophageal biopsies, VLEM as the only endoscopic abnormality was associated with histologic esophagitis: only 1 of 41 biopsies (2.4%) with VLEM was histologically normal, versus 57.5% of biopsies from endoscopically normal mucosa. Most children with VLEM had eosinophilic esophagitis (34 of 41, 83%), usually of moderate to severe intensity (31 of 34, 91.2%), supporting VLEM as an endoscopic marker of esophagitis. For eosinophilic esophagitis, VLEM had a specificity of 0.85 and a sensitivity of 0.5; for moderate to severe eosinophilic esophagitis, specificity was 0.88 and sensitivity 0.73.

question: Are head and neck specific quality of life measures necessary?
answer: In a cross-sectional study of 55 head and neck cancer patients, head and neck-specific health status domains were largely distinct from general QOL measures, which supports the need for head and neck-specific measures. The Head&Neck Survey correlated more strongly with the other head and neck-specific measures than with the general health measure. Eating/swallowing and speech/communication were not well correlated with general health domains, and appearance was not fully reflected by any other domain. Head and neck pain was highly correlated with general bodily pain (0.88), so the pain domain overlaps with general measures more than the other domains do.

question: Does the SCL 90-R obsessive-compulsive dimension identify cognitive impairments?
answer: In 19 adults with malignant brain tumors, the SCL 90-R Obsessive-Compulsive subscale was not related to objective measures of attention or verbal memory, so it did not identify objectively measured cognitive impairment. The subscale was instead strongly related to depression (r = .81), anxiety (r = .66), and subjective memory complaints (r = .75). Depression accounted for 66% of the variance in subscale scores, with anxiety adding 6%.

question: Hypotension in patients with coronary disease: can profound hypotensive events cause myocardial ischaemic events?
answer: In patients with ischaemic heart disease on hypotensive cardiovascular drugs, ST-segment ischaemic events were significantly associated with preceding ambulatory hypotensive events (chi2 = 40.2, p<0.0001), and 14 hypotension-induced ischaemic events occurred in 8 of 25 patients. 13 of the 14 hypotension-induced ischaemic events were preceded by a fall in diastolic pressure, and 6 by a fall in systolic pressure, suggesting diastolic hypotension is the more prominent precursor. All patients with hypotension-induced ischaemic events (8/8) were taking multiple hypotensive drug regimens, compared with 9/17 of those without such events (p = 0.022).

question: Fatigue in primary Sjögren's syndrome: is there a link with the fibromyalgia syndrome?
answer: Fatigue was common in primary Sjögren's syndrome (50/74, 68%), but fibromyalgia was present in only 9/74 (12%). Fibromyalgia therefore does not appear to account for most of the fatigue in pSS. Fatigue was significantly more prevalent in pSS than in lupus patients (68% vs 50%, p<0.0087). Fibromyalgia was numerically more frequent in pSS than in lupus (12% vs 5%) and was absent in the lupus patients with secondary Sjögren's syndrome (0 of 13, of whom 7 had fatigue).

question: Is alexithymia a risk factor for unexplained physical symptoms in general medical outpatients?
answer: In a cross-sectional study of 321 internal medicine outpatients, those with medically unexplained physical symptoms (169 patients) were overall not more alexithymic than those with explained symptoms, so alexithymia was not shown to be a risk factor. Among patients with unexplained symptoms, alexithymia was not associated with subjective health experience or use of medical services. Higher alexithymia was found only in a subgroup: patients with unexplained symptoms and a mental disorder who also denied any connection between emotional problems and their physical symptoms.

question: Is semi-closed endarterectomy of the superficial femoral artery combined with a short venous bypass in case of insufficient venous material an acceptable alternative for limb-threatening ischemia?
answer: In 30 patients with critical leg ischemia and insufficient vein, semiclosed SFA endarterectomy combined with a short venous bypass gave cumulative primary patency of 60.3% at 1 year and 48.4% at 3 years, with limb salvage of 68.6% at both 1 and 3 years.

question: Antral follicle assessment as a tool for predicting outcome in IVF--is it a better predictor than age and FSH?
answer: In a prospective study of 224 IVF patients, baseline antral follicle count >6 was associated with a much higher clinical pregnancy rate than count ≤6 (51% vs. 19%), and this difference remained significant after controlling for maternal age and basal FSH. Cycle cancellation was far more frequent with antral follicle count ≤6 than with a higher count (33% vs. 1%); cancellation also rose with advancing age and elevated basal FSH. In a separate cohort of women who conceived after IVF/ICSI, antral follicle count was the only ovarian reserve marker (compared with FSH, basal oestradiol and oestradiol response) that differed significantly between miscarriage and ongoing pregnancy, but its discriminative ability was low (AUC 0.588).

question: Acute respiratory distress syndrome in children with malignancy--can we predict outcome?
answer: In a retrospective review of 17 children with malignancy and ARDS requiring mechanical ventilation (6 survived, 35.3%), early ventilator measures (peak inspiratory pressure, PEEP, ventilation index) distinguished outcome by day 3. Oxygenation efficiency measures (PaO2/FIO2 and P(A-a)O2) were significantly related to outcome from day 8 after the start of mechanical ventilation.

question: Does tranexamic acid reduce desmopressin-induced hyperfibrinolysis?
answer: In a randomized trial of 100 CABG patients, adding tranexamic acid to desmopressin reduced fibrinolysis markers versus desmopressin alone: fibrin split products were lower (13.5 vs 21.2 ng/mL) and postoperative fibrinogen was higher (167 vs 113 mg/dL), both P=.0001. The combination was also associated with less postoperative drainage (623 vs 1010 mL), fewer units of red cells and fresh frozen plasma transfused, and a lower proportion of patients needing donor blood products (24% vs 74%). Postoperative hemoglobin was higher in the desmopressin plus tranexamic acid group (9.1 vs 7.6 g/dL, P=.0001).

question: Is specialty care associated with improved survival of patients with congestive heart failure?
answer: In a retrospective VHA cohort of 11,661 CHF patients, those with mixed general medicine and cardiology follow-up had the best 1-year survival. Adjusted risk of death was higher with general medicine only (RR 1.26, 1.15-1.38) and with neither clinic (RR 1.48, 1.28-1.72), compared with mixed care. Cardiology-only follow-up was not significantly different from mixed care (RR 1.12, 0.94-1.34). The survival difference between general medicine only and mixed care was reproduced in a second cohort (RR 1.25, 1.14-1.37). Unadjusted 1-year mortality was lowest in the mixed care group (19%) and highest in patients with no general medicine or cardiology follow-up (29%).

question: Locoregional opening of the rodent blood-brain barrier for paclitaxel using Nd:YAG laser-induced thermo therapy: a new concept of adjuvant glioma therapy?
answer: In rats, Nd:YAG laser-induced thermotherapy (LITT) of the forebrain opened the blood-brain barrier locally, shown by extravasation of Evans blue, C3C, fibrinogen and IgM, and HPLC confirmed that paclitaxel passed across the disrupted barrier into brain tissue. question: Can progression of valvar aortic stenosis be predicted accurately?
answer: The same cohort yielded concrete thresholds: progression rate depended on calcification grade (0 to III) and was exponentially correlated with initial aortic valve opening area. Falling below AVA 0.75 cm2 (VC 0), 0.8 (VC I), 0.9 (VC II) or 1.0 (VC III) made later surgery probable. Age, sex and etiology of the valvar obstruction did not significantly influence progression, so prediction rests mainly on calcification and hemodynamic measures.

question: Does early discharge with nurse home visits affect adequacy of newborn metabolic screening?
answer: Early discharge (24-47 hours) had mixed effects on newborn metabolic screening adequacy. More initial filter paper specimens were inadequate (22.9% vs 14.3% with traditional stay), but a higher share of early-discharge infants had an adequate specimen within 9 days (98.8% vs 96.7%). question: Sub-classification of low-grade cerebellar astrocytoma: is it clinically meaningful?
answer: In a Danish cohort of children with cerebellar astrocytoma, histological sub-classification had no prognostic value: survival did not differ between pilocytic and fibrillary astrocytoma, and the Kernohan and WHO systems had no predictive value. The Daumas-Duport grading system was found unsuitable as a prognostic tool for low-grade posterior fossa astrocytomas. Survival was instead associated with surgical gross-total removal and with tumor location in the cerebellum proper rather than the fourth ventricle, with overall survival of 81% after 15-40 years of follow-up.

question: Juvenile ankylosing spondylitis--is it the same disease as adult ankylosing spondylitis?
answer: In a retrospective review of 210 Indian patients with AS, juvenile-onset (n=60) and adult-onset (n=150) disease differed clinically, suggesting they are not identical presentations of the same disease. Juvenile-onset AS showed greater male preponderance, more frequent onset with peripheral arthritis, and greater hip and knee joint involvement than adult AS. Valvular dysfunction was seen only in patients with juvenile AS.
